Model risk review · Tier A

A dataset that scores 0.94 and predicts nothing

Loan Prediction Based on Customer Behavior — 252,000 applicant records, 11 attributes. Why the model this file produces cannot be deployed, and what to check before the next one.

Situation“Loan Prediction Based on Customer Behavior” is one of the most-worked credit datasets in public circulation — 252,000 labelled applicants, 11 demographic and stability attributes, zero missing values, zero duplicate rows. The standard result is a tree ensemble at roughly 93.6% AUC and 89.8% accuracy, comfortably above the 87.7% majority-class rate, and it is reproduced in notebook after notebook.

ComplicationThat result does not survive one check the standard workflow never runs. Id is unique on every row, so the duplicate test passes — but drop Id and 85.7% of the file is copies of other rows: 6,000 applicants replicated 27–40 times each. A random 5-fold split therefore trains and tests on the same applicants. Two further defects point the same way: the file is sorted into two blocks defaulting at 11.0% and 20.2% that no feature distinguishes, and the 28,000-row test set is 85.7% already present in the training file.

The 0.94-AUC classifier this dataset is known for is duplicate-row memorisation, not a model: measured on applicants rather than rows it ranks at 0.4987 [0.4917, 0.5059] — a coin flip — and a lender deploying it would decline applicants at random while reporting 89.8% accuracy to its model risk committee.

  1. The instrumentThe file is 42,007 applicants stretched to 252,000 rows. 6,000 profiles are replicated 27–40 times each (85.7% of rows), and Id being unique on every row is exactly why the standard duplicate check passes. The file is also sorted into two blocks defaulting at 11.0% and 20.2% that are statistically identical on every applicant attribute, the test set is 85.7% already in train, and 72.5% of test rows arrive in a category vocabulary the training file never uses.
  2. The signalMeasured at the applicant level there is none. Out-of-fold AUC on the 36,007 genuinely unique applicants is 0.4987 [0.4917, 0.5059]; grouped random forest scores 0.4913 and the replicated block scores 0.4912 — three disjoint measurements agreeing on chance. Not one of Profession, State or City survives a placebo permuted at the applicant level (p = 0.501, 0.131, 0.090) though all three pass at row level at z = +15 to +32.
  3. The consequenceRecall on defaulters falls from 0.477 to 0.001 when copies of one applicant are kept on one side of the split. The best honest model (logistic regression, 0.5184) is beaten by 0.6744 by Id — a row counter. And the resulting scorer declines the lowest-risk groups most: home owners default at 8.98% and are declined at 13.40%.

Recommendation — the model risk lead

  1. Reject the model and void the validation. The 5-fold cross-validation that produced its metrics is invalid on a replicated file. No re-tuning fixes this; the signal is not there to recover.
  2. Add the four-check audit to the model validation standard, as a pre-modelling gate. Duplicate check excluding surrogate keys; identifier-as-feature check; cross-file vocabulary check; holdout-membership check. All four are under ten lines and all four fired here.
  3. Require every validation to declare its unit of independence. Splits and permutation tests must group by that unit. On this file the row-level and applicant-level answers differ by 0.44 AUC and, for car ownership, by the sign of the effect.
  4. Require a naive baseline table that includes the row identifier. Any model that cannot beat the row number has not been validated, it has been scored.
  5. Source a real credit file before resuming applicant-scoring work. With loan terms, repayment history and timestamps — the fields the data assessment (§3) already identified as missing. No amount of cleaning turns this file into a model.
So what
The headline exhibit: one file, one model, one seed, and a 0.44 AUC gap that depends entirely on whether the validation split respected the unit of independence.

Part I · The instrument

All four pre-modelling checks fail, and the one that matters passes by accident

Pre-modelling checkResultFinding
Duplicate rows excluding identifier columnsFAIL85.71% of rows duplicated; 42,007 distinct applicants
Score the identifier as a featureFAILId alone reaches AUC 0.6744
Category vocabulary, train vs testFAIL47 test-only categories; 72.45% of test rows affected
Holdout membership in trainFAIL24,003 of 28,000 test rows (85.72%) already in train

This file has 42,007 applicants, not 252,000 — 6,000 of them appear 27 to 40 times each

So what
A random 5-fold split places copies of the same applicant in the training fold and the validation fold, so the model is scored on rows it has memorised. drop_duplicates() removes nothing, because Id is unique on all 252,000 rows. The group-size distribution is bimodal with nothing between 2 and 26 copies — a generator loop, not a data-entry accident.

The file is sorted into two blocks whose applicants are identical and whose default rates differ by 83%

So what
Income is indistinguishable across the two blocks (KS p = 0.17) and Age, Experience and both tenure columns agree to within 1.5%. The default rate differs by a factor of 1.8. Two label-generating regimes were applied to one applicant population, and no attribute tracks which regime a row came from — only its row number does.

72% of the test set arrives in a vocabulary the model has never seen — and that conceals an 86% overlap

So what
Train writes Software_Developer; test writes Software Developer. 23 of 51 professions and 8 of 29 states differ by a separator alone, so an encoder fitted on train silently maps 72.5% of test rows to “unknown”. It also means an analyst checking whether the holdout is genuinely held out gets back 23.7% instead of the true 85.7%.

Every categorical driver is decisive at row level and indistinguishable from noise at applicant level

So what
Permuting 2,000 times at the row level puts all three columns 15 to 32 standard deviations above their null. Permuting whole applicants — the only unit this file supports — gives p = 0.501 (Profession), 0.131 (State) and 0.090 (City); none significant, before or after Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Replication multiplies n sixfold without adding one bit of information, and χ² scales with n.

No demographic, tenure or asset cut moves the default rate more than 27%

So what
The largest effect anywhere is home ownership — owners at 8.98% against renters at 12.56%. Every numeric feature has |Cohen's d| below 0.029, two orders of magnitude under the “small effect” threshold. And the pooled effects that do reach significance disappear on the clean sub-sample: home ownership becomes +0.82pp [-1.05, +2.70], and car ownership changes sign, significantly, in both directions.

Part III · The consequence

The same model, three ways of measuring it

36,007 unique applicants — nothing can leak0.4987——

The same model scores 0.94 and 0.49 depending only on whether copies of one applicant may sit on both sides of the split

So what
Random forest, identical features, identical seed: 0.936 under a row split, 0.491 grouped by applicant. Accuracy falls from 0.898 to 0.877 — exactly the majority-class rate. The third scheme removes the last excuse: on the 36,007 applicants who appear once, where nothing can leak and no grouping is involved, every model lands at 0.50.

The row number predicts default better than income, age, profession, city and state combined

So what
Id reaches AUC 0.674; the best honest model built from all 11 attributes reaches 0.518. Any validation standard that would have approved the 0.936 model must also explain why it did not catch the row counter — both come from the same two lines of missing diagnostics.

Under an honest split no threshold trades precision for recall

So what
The precision–recall curve sits flat on the 12.3% base rate across the whole recall range: precision never exceeds what declining at random achieves. The data assessment's operating-threshold question (§4) has an answer, and the answer is that there is no threshold worth choosing. Class balancing moves recall from 0.004 to 0.275 and leaves AUC at 0.50 — it changes where the threshold sits, not whether the score ranks.

A chance-level scorer reporting 90% accuracy declines the groups that default least

So what
9 of 17 subgroups are declined more often than they default, and they include the four lowest-risk groups in the file. Across all subgroups the correlation between how often a group defaults and how often it is declined is +0.15 — essentially unrelated. This is disparate impact with no accuracy defence available: the usual justification for declining a group more is that it defaults more, and here the opposite holds.

Appendix · Method and limits

What this analysis does not claim

No null result here transfers to real credit portfolios. Income and employment stability are well-established credit predictors in real lending books. This file is synthetic: Income, Age and Experience are mutually uncorrelated (|r| ≤ 0.007) and near-uniform, and 32,189 rows (12.8%) imply a career starting before age 18, the youngest at 1. Every claim above is bounded to this instrument.

No metric anywhere in this project is computed against Test Data.csv. There is no ground truth for it. Sample Prediction Dataset.csv is random noise — 12.8% positive, AUC 0.504 against every feature — so it is a formatting template, not a benchmark, and calibrating a threshold to its positive rate would be calibrating to nothing. Every performance figure above comes from cross-validation inside the training file.

Causal inference is out of scope and stays out. There is no treatment, no assignment mechanism, no timestamp, no instrument and no discontinuity. Nothing above is a causal estimate.

The ceiling, for completeness. Knowing exactly which of the 6,000 replicated applicants a row belongs to explains 54.1% of its label — the generator assigned the rest by a per-row coin flip. Even a perfect lookup misclassifies 16,247 rows by construction. Applicant identity is not a feature; it is 42,007 hashes, unavailable for anyone new.

Reproducibility. Six numbered notebooks, run in order, RANDOM_STATE = 42 throughout, restart-and-run-all verified from the raw CSVs. No local module imports — chart styling, the audit checks and the placebo harness are defined inline in each notebook so a fresh clone runs on the pinned packages alone. Every number in this report is read from reports/_key_figures.json, written by notebooks 01–05; nothing here is hardcoded.

Source: Kaggle “Loan Prediction Based on Customer Behavior” (Univ.AI hackathon, synthetic) — 252,000 training rows, 28,000 test rows. Analysis 2026-08-01. Built to the McKinsey communication standard per DOCS/STRUCTURE.md; visual system per DOCS/DESIGN.md.
